The operating frequency was 25.9 MHz with a wavelength of 38 feet
The transmitter was positioned 300 feet from the target
The transmitting antenna was a half-wave loaded dipole, 10 feet long, mounted 10 feet above ground
The probe antenna was 5 feet 3 inches long, mounted 8 feet above ground
The probe was typically positioned 20-60 feet from the target
Measurements were taken at intervals of 2.5 feet along the transmitter-target line
The 25.9-MHz amplifier had a gain of 80 dB and 3-dB bandwidth of 180 kHz
The telemeter operated at 10.177 MHz
A typical data set for a given target could be obtained in 15 minutes
94% of probe readings had deviations less than 1.1% (0.1 dB) from the mean
The voltage comparator null could always be found below -16 dB
For a half-wave dipole, σ/λ² = 0.88
Resonance maxima in dipole RCS occurred at lengths of λ/2, 3λ/2, and higher odd multiples
The measured cross section of a 30-foot target was estimated to be about 10% too small due to non-plane-wave reception
Mercury batteries were used throughout the probe system to ensure constant voltage
The probe antenna and telemetering antenna were short enough to have negligible effect on measured fields
Dipoles shorter than 10 feet had cross sections too small to be measured by the system
Three oak trees were used as radar targets and designated Tree I, II, and III
A street light and truck were also measured as radar targets
The test site was a level, ploughed field free of trees except for isolated oak trees
The high-frequency range of interest was 3 to 30 MHz
A man was assigned a standard position 15 feet from the probe to minimize parasitic effects
Temperature drift in the probe was negligible in warmer months with proper thermistor adjustment
The transmitter could deliver 350 watts of continuous-wave power to the coaxial line
Ferrite cylinders were used to shield the coaxial line near the transmitting antenna
